learn.hook: 'Mangoes are the best fruit' starts an argument. '7 is a prime number' ends one. Maths loves sentences that are clearly true or clearly false!
points: A proposition (mathematical statement) is a sentence that is either true or false, but not both.
Questions, commands, exclamations and opinions are not propositions: 'Is 5 odd?', 'Shut the door', 'Maths is fun'.
A sentence like x + 3 = 7 is an open sentence: it becomes true or false only once x is known.
Many propositions have the form 'If P, then Q'. P is the hypothesis and Q is the conclusion.
A statement about ALL cases is false if even one counterexample exists. The negation of 'All birds can fly' is 'Some birds cannot fly' (not 'No birds can fly').

example.q: Is 'Every odd number is prime' a proposition? Is it true?
steps: It makes a clear claim that is either true or false, so it is a proposition
Test: 9 is odd, but 9 = 3 × 3 is not prime
One counterexample is enough, so the statement is false
example.answer: It is a proposition, and it is false (counterexample: 9)

learn.reallife: Courts, contracts and computer programs all rely on statements that must be clearly true or false. 'If the PIN is correct, then open the account' is a proposition in code!

games.title: Proposition or not?
items: 7 is a prime number
The sum of the angles of a triangle is 200°
Every square is a rectangle
Is 15 divisible by 3?
Please solve this sum
Cricket is the most exciting sport
What a lovely rangoli!

games.title: Judge the statement
items: Every square is a rectangle
A square has four right angles and opposite sides equal, so it fits the definition of a rectangle.
Every rectangle is a square
A 4 cm by 2 cm rectangle is a counterexample: its sides are not all equal.
2 is the only even prime number
Every other even number is divisible by 2, so it has at least three factors.
The sum of two odd numbers is odd
3 + 5 = 8, which is even. In fact the sum of two odd numbers is always even.
'2 + 2 = 5' is not a proposition because it is false
False sentences are still propositions. A proposition just has to be true or false.
The square of any real number is never negative
Positive × positive and negative × negative are both positive, and 0² = 0.

quiz.q: Which of these is a proposition?
quiz.explain: '7 is a prime number' is definitely true or false (it is true). The others are a command, a question and an opinion.
steps: A proposition is either true or false, not both.
'Close the window' is a command; 'Is 5 odd?' is a question; 'tastiest fruit' is an opinion.
'7 is a prime number' is definitely true.
Answer: 7 is a prime number
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence with a number in it is a proposition

quiz.q: Which proposition is false?
options: The angles of a triangle add up to 200°
quiz.explain: The angles of a triangle always add up to 180°, so the statement about 200° is false.
steps: 2 is an even prime: true. Every square is a rectangle: true. √9 = 3: true.
The angles of a triangle add up to 180°, not 200°.
Answer: The angles of a triangle add up to 200°
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'every square is a rectangle' is false because squares and rectangles have different names

quiz.q: What is the negation of 'All birds can fly'?
quiz.explain: To deny 'all', you only need at least one exception. Penguins and ostriches show some birds cannot fly.
steps: To deny 'all', we need at least one exception.
'Some birds cannot fly' (e.g. penguins) is the negation.
'No birds can fly' is too strong.
Answer: Some birds cannot fly
quiz.mistake: Thinks the opposite of 'all' is 'none'

quiz.q: Which number is a counterexample to 'Every odd number is prime'?
quiz.explain: 9 is odd but not prime, since 9 = 3 × 3. A counterexample must satisfy the 'if' part and break the claim.
steps: A counterexample must be odd and not prime.
7 and 3 are odd primes; 2 is not odd.
9 is odd and 9 = 3 × 3 is not prime.
Answer: 9
quiz.mistake: Picks 2, which is prime but not odd, so it does not test the claim

quiz.q: In 'If a number ends in 0, then it is divisible by 5', what is the hypothesis?
quiz.explain: The hypothesis is the 'if' part: a number ends in 0. The conclusion is the 'then' part.
steps: In 'If P, then Q', P is the hypothesis.
Here P = 'a number ends in 0'; Q = 'it is divisible by 5'.
Answer: A number ends in 0
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the hypothesis (if part) with the conclusion (then part)

quiz.q: Is 'x + 3 = 7' a proposition?
options: Not on its own; it becomes true or false only once x is known
No, because it has an equals sign
quiz.explain: It is true when x = 4 and false otherwise, so on its own it is an open sentence.
steps: x + 3 = 7 is true when x = 4 and false otherwise.
On its own it is an open sentence, not a proposition.
Answer: Not on its own; it becomes true or false only once x is known
quiz.mistake: Thinks every equation is automatically a true statement

quiz.q: Which whole number is a counterexample to 'n² > n for every whole number n'?
quiz.explain: 1² = 1, which is not greater than 1. (0 also works.) For 3, 5 and 10 the claim holds.
steps: Test n = 1: 1² = 1, which is not greater than 1.
So 1 is a counterexample.
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Tests only large numbers, where the claim happens to be true

quiz.q: Riya says 'Every rectangle is a square.' Which reply proves her wrong?
options: A 4 cm × 4 cm square is a rectangle
A 4 cm × 2 cm rectangle is not a square
quiz.explain: One rectangle that is not a square is a counterexample, and that is enough to show the claim is false.
steps: To disprove 'every rectangle is a square', give one rectangle that is not a square.
A 4 cm × 2 cm rectangle has unequal sides, so it is not a square.
Answer: A 4 cm × 2 cm rectangle is not a square
quiz.mistake: Gives an example that agrees with the claim, which cannot disprove it

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: "Is 'Laddoos are yummy' a mathematical statement? It sounds true to me!"
teach.praise: A proposition must be clearly true or false, not both. 'Laddoos are yummy' is an opinion, so it isn't one, even if I agree!
teach.nudge: Can everyone agree whether 'laddoos are yummy' is true or false? What must a proposition always be?

revise.summary: A proposition is a sentence that is either true or false. Questions, commands and opinions are not propositions; 'If P, then Q' has hypothesis P and conclusion Q. One counterexample disproves an 'all' statement.
focus: Disprove with a counterexample and negate 'all'.
remember: x + 3 = 7 is an open sentence.
Negation of 'All birds can fly': 'Some birds cannot fly'.
'Every odd number is prime' is false: 9.
traps: The opposite of 'all' is 'some ... not', not 'none'.
A counterexample must satisfy the 'if' part.
An example that agrees cannot disprove a claim.

learn.hook: 'If you are in Jaipur, you are in Rajasthan' is true. But 'If you are in Rajasthan, you are in Jaipur'? Swapping can change everything!
points: The converse of 'If P, then Q' is 'If Q, then P': the hypothesis and conclusion swap places.
A true statement can have a false converse. 'If a number is divisible by 4, it is even' is true, but 6 is even and not divisible by 4.
Some statements and their converses are both true, such as Pythagoras' theorem and its converse.
When a statement and its converse are both true, we can join them with 'if and only if'.
To show a converse is false, give one counterexample: a case where Q is true but P is false.

example.q: Write the converse of 'If x = 3, then x² = 9' and decide whether it is true.
steps: Swap the parts: 'If x² = 9, then x = 3'
Test x = −3: (−3)² = 9, but x is not 3
So the converse is false
example.answer: Converse: If x² = 9, then x = 3. It is false (x = −3).

learn.reallife: 'If it is a mango, it is a fruit' is true, but 'If it is a fruit, it is a mango' would leave the banana seller very upset!

games.title: Match each statement with its converse
pairs: If it rains, the ground gets wet
If the ground gets wet, it rains
If n is divisible by 6, n is divisible by 3
If n is divisible by 3, n is divisible by 6
If a shape is a square, it has four sides
If a shape has four sides, it is a square
If x = 5, then 2x = 10
If 2x = 10, then x = 5
If I am in Pune, I am in Maharashtra
If I am in Maharashtra, I am in Pune

games.title: Is the converse true?
items: If x = 5, then 2x = 10
If a triangle has three equal sides, it has three equal angles
If a number is a multiple of 10, it ends in 0
If n is divisible by 6, n is divisible by 3
If a shape is a square, it has four sides
If x = 3, then x² = 9
If I am in Pune, I am in Maharashtra

quiz.q: What is the converse of 'If it is raining, then the ground is wet'?
options: If it is not raining, the ground is not wet
If the ground is wet, then it is raining
If the ground is not wet, it is not raining
It is raining and the ground is wet
quiz.explain: The converse swaps the hypothesis and the conclusion.
steps: The converse of 'If P, then Q' is 'If Q, then P'.
P = it is raining; Q = the ground is wet.
Converse: If the ground is wet, then it is raining.
Answer: If the ground is wet, then it is raining
quiz.mistake: Adds 'not' to both parts instead of swapping them

quiz.q: 'If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even' is true. What about its converse?
options: True, because 8 is even and divisible by 4
False, because 6 is even but not divisible by 4
quiz.explain: The converse is 'If a number is even, it is divisible by 4'. The even number 6 is not divisible by 4, so the converse is false.
steps: Converse: 'If a number is even, it is divisible by 4.'
6 is even, but 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5.
One counterexample makes the converse false.
Answer: False, because 6 is even but not divisible by 4
quiz.mistake: Thinks one example that works (like 8) proves a statement for all numbers

quiz.q: Which statement has a TRUE converse?
options: If a quadrilateral is a square, it has four right angles
If a triangle has three equal sides, it has three equal angles
If n is divisible by 6, then n is divisible by 3
quiz.explain: A triangle with three equal angles also has three equal sides, so this converse is true. The others fail: x = −3, a rectangle, and n = 9.
steps: Converses: 'x² = 9 ⇒ x = 3' fails (x = −3); 'four right angles ⇒ square' fails (rectangle).
'Divisible by 3 ⇒ divisible by 6' fails (n = 9).
'Three equal angles ⇒ three equal sides' is true.
Answer: If a triangle has three equal sides, it has three equal angles
quiz.mistake: Assumes that if a statement is true, its converse must be true too

quiz.q: Which value of x shows that 'If x² = 9, then x = 3' is false?
quiz.explain: (−3)² = 9, so the 'if' part holds, but x is not 3.
steps: We need x² = 9 but x ≠ 3.
Answer: −3
quiz.mistake: Picks 3, which agrees with the statement instead of breaking it

quiz.q: 'If two angles are vertically opposite, then they are equal' is true. Is its converse true?
options: Yes, equal angles are always vertically opposite
No, two angles can be equal without being vertically opposite
Yes, but only for right angles
quiz.explain: The converse says 'If two angles are equal, they are vertically opposite'. Two 60° angles in an equilateral triangle are equal but not vertically opposite.
steps: Converse: 'If two angles are equal, they are vertically opposite.'
Two 60° angles of an equilateral triangle are equal but not vertically opposite.
So the converse is false.
Answer: No, two angles can be equal without being vertically opposite
quiz.mistake: Assumes every true statement has a true converse

quiz.q: By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, which triangle is right-angled?
quiz.explain: 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². When the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side, the triangle is right-angled.
steps: Equal, so there is a right angle opposite the side 25
Answer: 7, 24, 25
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of their squares

quiz.q: 'A triangle is equilateral if and only if all its angles are 60°.' What does 'if and only if' tell us?
options: Both the statement and its converse are true
quiz.explain: 'If and only if' joins a statement with its converse when both are true.
steps: 'If and only if' joins a statement with its converse.
It is used only when both directions are true.
Answer: Both the statement and its converse are true
quiz.mistake: Reads 'if and only if' as just 'if'

quiz.q: 'If n is odd, then n² is odd' is true. Is its converse 'If n² is odd, then n is odd' true?
options: Yes: if n were even, n² would be even, so n must be odd
No: 9 is odd but 3 is not
No: the converse of a true statement is always false
quiz.explain: If n were even, n² = n × n would be even. So whenever n² is odd, n must be odd. Both directions are true.
steps: Suppose n² is odd. If n were even, n × n would be even.
That contradicts n² odd, so n must be odd.
So the converse is true too.
Answer: Yes: if n were even, n² would be even, so n must be odd
quiz.mistake: Thinks converses are always false, which is just as wrong as thinking they are always true

teach.ask: Gappu says: "'If it is a parrot, it is a bird' is true. So 'If it is a bird, it is a parrot' must also be true, right?"
teach.praise: The converse swaps the two parts, and it can be false. A crow is a bird but not a parrot! Thanks for saving me from a silly mistake.
teach.nudge: What happens when you swap the 'if' and 'then' parts? Can you think of a bird that is not a parrot?

revise.summary: The converse of 'If P, then Q' is 'If Q, then P'. A true statement can have a false converse; when both are true we say 'if and only if'.
remember: 'Divisible by 4 ⇒ even' is true; its converse fails at 6.
'x = 3 ⇒ x² = 9': converse fails at x = −3.
'n odd ⇔ n² odd' is true both ways.
traps: Swap the parts; don't add 'not'.
A true statement's converse is not automatically true.
Converses are not always false either.

learn.hook: Equal sides give equal angles. Do equal angles give equal sides? Geometry says yes, but it needs a proof!
points: Proposition: if two sides of a triangle are equal, the angles opposite them are equal. Its converse: if two angles are equal, the sides opposite them are equal. Both are true.
Proof idea for the converse: in △ABC with ∠B = ∠C, drop the altitude AD. △ABD ≅ △ACD (AAS: ∠B = ∠C, right angles at D, AD common), so AB = AC.
Congruent triangles always have equal areas, but the converse is false: a triangle with base 6 and height 4 and one with base 8 and height 3 both have area 12 but are not congruent.

Converse of Baudhayana–Pythagoras: if a² + b² = c² in a triangle, the angle opposite c is 90°. Proof: build a right triangle with legs a and b; its hypotenuse is √(a² + b²) = c, so the two triangles are congruent by SSS and the original angle is also 90°.

example.q: Is a triangle with sides 9, 40 and 41 right-angled? Which angle is 90°?
steps: Equal, so by the converse the angle opposite 41 is 90°
example.answer: Yes; the angle opposite the side 41

learn.reallife: Carpenters check a right corner with a 3-4-5 rope: that's the converse of Pythagoras in action.

games.title: Geometry converses
items: If two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides opposite them are equal.
Proved using an altitude and congruence.
If two triangles have equal areas, they are congruent.
Base 6, height 4 and base 8, height 3 both give 12.
If a² + b² = c², the triangle has a right angle opposite c.
Converse of Baudhayana–Pythagoras.
Congruent triangles have equal areas.
They cover exactly the same space.
Sides 5, 6, 7 form a right triangle.

quiz.q: In △PQR, ∠Q = ∠R = 65° and PQ = 9 cm. What is PR?
quiz.explain: Sides opposite equal angles are equal: PR (opposite ∠Q) = PQ (opposite ∠R).
steps: Sides opposite equal angles are equal.
PR is opposite ∠Q; PQ is opposite ∠R; ∠Q = ∠R.
So PR = PQ = 9 cm.
Answer: 9 cm
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal angles say nothing about sides

quiz.q: To prove 'equal angles ⇒ equal opposite sides' in △ABC with ∠B = ∠C, which line is drawn?
options: The altitude AD from A to BC
quiz.explain: The altitude gives two right triangles that can be shown congruent.
steps: Draw the altitude AD from A to BC.
It makes two right triangles ABD and ACD that can be shown congruent.
Answer: The altitude AD from A to BC
quiz.mistake: Draws a line that creates no congruent triangles

quiz.q: In that proof, △ABD ≅ △ACD by which rule?
quiz.explain: ∠B = ∠C, ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°, and side AD is common.
steps: In △ABD and △ACD: ∠B = ∠C, ∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°.
Side AD is common (not between the two angles).
Angle, angle, side: AAS.
Answer: AAS
quiz.mistake: Uses SSS though AB = AC is what we want to prove

quiz.q: Which pair of triangles shows that equal area does not imply congruence?
options: Base 4, height 6 and base 4, height 6 (same shape)
quiz.explain: Both have area 15 but different bases, so they cannot be congruent.
steps: Base 10, height 3: area ½ × 10 × 3 = 15.
Base 6, height 5: area ½ × 6 × 5 = 15.
Equal areas but different bases, so not congruent.
Answer: Base 10, height 3 and base 6, height 5
quiz.mistake: Picks triangles that are actually congruent

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 20, 21 and 29. Is it right-angled?
steps: Answer: Yes, 20² + 21² = 29²
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of their squares

quiz.q: In the proof of the Pythagoras converse, why are the original triangle and the constructed right triangle congruent?
options: SSS: a, b equal by construction and both third sides equal c
quiz.explain: The constructed hypotenuse is √(a² + b²) = c, so all three sides match.
steps: Constructed right triangle has legs a and b, hypotenuse √(a² + b²) = c.
The original triangle has sides a, b, c.
All three sides match: SSS.
Answer: SSS: a, b equal by construction and both third sides equal c
quiz.mistake: Assumes the right angle in the original triangle, which is what we want to prove

quiz.q: Which statement is the converse of 'If a triangle is right-angled with hypotenuse c, then a² + b² = c²'?
options: If a² + b² ≠ c², it is not right-angled
If the triangle is not right-angled, a² + b² ≠ c²
If a² + b² = c², then the triangle is right-angled with hypotenuse c
If c² = a² − b², it is right-angled
quiz.explain: The converse swaps hypotenuse-condition and equation.
steps: Converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion.
Hypothesis becomes a² + b² = c²; conclusion becomes 'right-angled with hypotenuse c'.
Answer: If a² + b² = c², then the triangle is right-angled with hypotenuse c
quiz.mistake: Confuses the converse with the contrapositive or inverse

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 7, 8 and 11. What can you say?
options: It is right-angled at the largest angle
quiz.explain: The squares of the two smaller sides must add to the square of the largest.
steps: Squares of the two smaller sides: 7² + 8² = 49 + 64 = 113.
Square of the largest: 11² = 121.
113 ≠ 121, so it is not right-angled.
Answer: It is not right-angled, since 49 + 64 = 113 ≠ 121
quiz.mistake: Checks the wrong pair of sides

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If two angles of a triangle are equal, must the opposite sides be equal? How do you know?"
teach.praise: Superb! Drop the altitude, prove the triangles congruent by AAS, and the sides are equal!
teach.nudge: What line could you draw from the top vertex? Which congruence rule helps?

revise.summary: In a triangle, equal sides face equal angles and equal angles face equal sides. Equal area does not imply congruence. The converse of Baudhayana–Pythagoras is true: a² + b² = c² means a right angle opposite c.
focus: Prove it with an altitude and AAS.
Test triangles with the Pythagoras converse.
remember: △ABD ≅ △ACD by AAS gives AB = AC.
Base 6, height 4 and base 8, height 3: both area 12, not congruent.
9, 40, 41: 81 + 1600 = 1681 = 41², right angle opposite 41.
traps: Don't use SSS when AB = AC is what you are proving.
Equal area does not mean congruent.
Compare the two smaller squares with the largest.

topics.title: Number converses: both true, both false

learn.hook: Count the factors of 16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Five, an odd number! Only perfect squares do that.
points: A proposition and its converse can both be true: 'If n is a perfect square, it has an odd number of factors' and 'If n has an odd number of factors, it is a perfect square'. Factors pair up as d and n/d, except √n, which pairs with itself.
Both can be false: 'If a number is a multiple of 3, it is even' (3 is a counterexample) and its converse 'If a number is even, it is a multiple of 3' (2 is a counterexample).
The square of a prime p has exactly 3 divisors: 1, p, p². Conversely, a number with exactly 3 divisors is the square of a prime.
A product of two distinct primes pq has exactly 4 divisors: 1, p, q, pq. But the converse fails: 8 has 4 divisors (1, 2, 4, 8) and is not a product of two distinct primes.

example.q: How many factors does 36 have? Is the count odd?
steps: 6 × 6 uses only one factor, 6
example.answer: 9, odd, since 36 is a perfect square

learn.reallife: Locker puzzles: if students toggle lockers by their factors, only lockers with perfect-square numbers end up open, because they have an odd number of factors.

games.title: Odd or even number of factors?

quiz.q: How many factors does 49 have?
quiz.explain: 1, 7, 49: the square of the prime 7.
steps: Factors of 49: 1, 7, 49.
49 = 7², the square of a prime.
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 1 and 49 are factors

quiz.q: Which number has an odd number of factors?
quiz.explain: 64 = 8² is a perfect square, so its factor 8 pairs with itself.
steps: A number has an odd number of factors exactly when it is a perfect square.
24, 50, 18 are not perfect squares; 64 = 8².
Answer: 64
quiz.mistake: Thinks large numbers always have even counts

quiz.q: 'If a number is a multiple of 3, then it is even.' Which number is a counterexample?
quiz.explain: 9 is a multiple of 3 but odd.
steps: We need a multiple of 3 that is not even.
6 and 12 are even; 4 is not a multiple of 3.
9 = 3 × 3 is odd.
Answer: 9
quiz.mistake: Gives a number that fits both parts

quiz.q: The converse 'If a number is even, then it is a multiple of 3' is:
quiz.explain: 4 is even but not a multiple of 3.
steps: Converse: 'If a number is even, it is a multiple of 3.'
4 is even but 4 ÷ 3 is not whole.
Answer: false, e.g. 4
quiz.mistake: Tests only one supporting example

quiz.q: How many divisors does 77 = 7 × 11 have?
steps: 77 = 7 × 11, two distinct primes.
Divisors: 1, 7, 11, 77.
Answer: 4
quiz.mistake: Counts only the primes

quiz.q: Which number shows that 'If n has exactly 4 divisors, then n is a product of two distinct primes' is false?
quiz.explain: 27 = 3³ has divisors 1, 3, 9, 27: four, but it is not pq.
steps: We need 4 divisors but not of the form pq.
27 = 3³ has divisors 1, 3, 9, 27: four.
Answer: 27
quiz.mistake: Picks a number that really is pq

quiz.q: A number has exactly 3 divisors. What must it be?
options: A product of two distinct primes
quiz.explain: Only p² has the divisors 1, p, p².
steps: Exactly 3 divisors: 1, p and p².
Only the square of a prime has this.
Answer: The square of a prime
quiz.mistake: Thinks primes have 3 divisors

quiz.q: Why does a perfect square have an odd number of factors?
options: Its square root is a factor that pairs with itself
quiz.explain: All other factors pair as d and n/d; √n is the unpaired one.
steps: Factors pair as d and n/d.
For a perfect square, √n pairs with itself.
So one factor is unpaired, giving an odd count.
Answer: Its square root is a factor that pairs with itself
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'odd number of factors' with 'odd number'

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Why do only perfect squares have an odd number of factors?"
teach.praise: Excellent! Factors come in pairs, but the square root pairs with itself!
teach.nudge: How do factors usually come? Which factor of 16 has no partner?

revise.summary: Some statements and converses are both true (perfect squares ⇔ odd number of factors); some are both false. p² has exactly 3 divisors; pq has 4, but having 4 divisors does not mean pq.
focus: Test statements and converses about divisors.
remember: 36 has 9 factors (odd) because 6 × 6 pairs with itself.
Exactly 3 divisors ⇔ square of a prime.
8 and 27 have 4 divisors but are not pq.
traps: Count 1 and the number itself as factors.
'Odd number of factors' is not 'odd number'.
Test both directions separately.

learn.hook: Two sticks crossing at their midpoints make a parallelogram. Make the sticks equal and you get a rectangle!
points: Parallel lines: if two lines are parallel, corresponding angles made by a transversal are equal; and conversely, equal corresponding angles mean the lines are parallel. Both directions are true.
'If a quadrilateral is a square, all its angles are equal' is true, but the converse fails: a rectangle has all angles equal and need not be a square.

In △ABC let the bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at the incentre I and cut AC at E and AB at F. 'If AB = AC, then IE = IF' is true: ∠B = ∠C gives ∠IBC = ∠ICB, so IB = IC, and then △IBF ≅ △ICE (ASA). Its converse 'If IE = IF, then AB = AC' is false: in a triangle with ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 90°, ∠C = 30°, IE = IF but AB ≠ AC.

Two sticks as diagonals joined at their midpoints always give a parallelogram; equal sticks give a rectangle; equal sticks crossing at right angles give a square. But 'equal diagonals ⇒ rectangle' fails if the diagonals do not bisect each other (an isosceles trapezium).

example.q: Write the converse of 'If a quadrilateral is a rectangle, its diagonals are equal' and test it.
steps: Converse: If a quadrilateral has equal diagonals, it is a rectangle
An isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals but is not a rectangle
So the converse is false

learn.reallife: Kite-makers use two crossing sticks: equal sticks crossing at their middles give a rectangular frame.

pairs: Bisect each other
Parallelogram
Equal and bisect each other
Rectangle

Rhombus
Equal, bisect each other at right angles

games.title: Is the converse true?
items: If lines are parallel, corresponding angles are equal
If it is a square, all angles are 90°
If AB = AC, the bisector pieces IE and IF are equal
If it is a rectangle, its diagonals are equal
If alternate angles are equal, the lines are parallel

quiz.q: 'If corresponding angles are equal, then the lines are parallel.' What is the converse and is it true?
options: If lines are parallel, corresponding angles are equal: true
If lines are not parallel, angles are equal: true
If angles are unequal, lines are parallel: false
quiz.explain: Both directions hold for parallel lines and a transversal.
steps: Converse swaps the parts: 'If lines are parallel, corresponding angles are equal.'
This is true; both directions hold.
Answer: If lines are parallel, corresponding angles are equal: true
quiz.mistake: Writes the inverse instead of the converse

quiz.q: Which shape shows that 'If all angles of a quadrilateral are equal, it is a square' is false?
options: A rectangle with sides 4 cm and 7 cm
quiz.explain: All its angles are 90° but its sides are not all equal.
steps: We need all angles equal but not a square.
A 4 cm × 7 cm rectangle has four 90° angles but unequal sides.
Answer: A rectangle with sides 4 cm and 7 cm
quiz.mistake: Picks a shape whose angles are not all equal

quiz.q: In △ABC with AB = AC, the bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at I and cut AC at E and AB at F. Why is IE = IF?
options: Because I is the midpoint of BE
Because BE is perpendicular to AC
∠IBC = ∠ICB, so IB = IC; then △IBF ≅ △ICE by ASA
Because IE = IF in every triangle
quiz.explain: Equal base angles have equal halves, so △IBC is isosceles with IB = IC. With the vertically opposite angles at I and the equal half-angles at B and C, ASA gives △IBF ≅ △ICE, so IF = IE.
steps: AB = AC gives ∠B = ∠C, so their halves ∠IBC = ∠ICB.
So IB = IC (△IBC is isosceles).
With ∠IBF = ∠ICE and vertically opposite ∠BIF = ∠CIE, △IBF ≅ △ICE (ASA), so IF = IE.
Answer: ∠IBC = ∠ICB, so IB = IC; then △IBF ≅ △ICE by ASA
quiz.mistake: Cannot pick the congruence that links IE and IF

quiz.q: In △ABC with ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 90° and ∠C = 30°, the same lengths IE and IF turn out to be equal. What does this show about the converse 'If IE = IF, then AB = AC'?
options: It is true only for right triangles
It is false: here IE = IF but AB ≠ AC
quiz.explain: AB is opposite the 30° angle and AC is opposite the 90° angle, so AB ≠ AC even though IE = IF. One counterexample is enough to make the converse false.
steps: In this triangle IE = IF.
AB is opposite 30° and AC is opposite 90°, so AB ≠ AC.
One counterexample makes the converse false.
Answer: It is false: here IE = IF but AB ≠ AC
quiz.mistake: Believes the converse of a true statement must be true

quiz.q: Two unequal sticks are joined at their midpoints at an angle that is not 90°. Their ends form a:
quiz.explain: Diagonals bisecting each other give a parallelogram; unequal and not perpendicular rules out the others.
steps: Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram.
Unequal diagonals rule out a rectangle; not perpendicular rules out a rhombus.
Answer: parallelogram
quiz.mistake: Assumes crossing sticks always give a rectangle

quiz.q: Two equal sticks are joined at their midpoints. Their ends always form a:
quiz.explain: Equal diagonals that bisect each other give a rectangle (a square if also perpendicular).
steps: Joined at midpoints: diagonals bisect each other, a parallelogram.
Equal diagonals make that parallelogram a rectangle.
Answer: rectangle
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal diagonals give a rhombus

quiz.q: Which quadrilateral has equal diagonals but is not a rectangle?
quiz.explain: Its diagonals are equal but they do not bisect each other.
steps: An isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals.
But its diagonals do not bisect each other, so it is not a rectangle.
Answer: An isosceles trapezium
quiz.mistake: Picks a shape with unequal diagonals

quiz.q: A transversal makes corresponding angles of 72° and 75° with two lines. What can you conclude?
quiz.explain: If the lines were parallel, corresponding angles would be equal.
steps: If the lines were parallel, corresponding angles would be equal.
So the lines are not parallel.
Answer: The lines are not parallel
quiz.mistake: Thinks nearly equal angles are enough

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If a quadrilateral has all angles equal, is it a square?"
teach.praise: Right! A rectangle has equal angles but isn't a square, so the converse fails!
teach.nudge: Can you think of a shape with four right angles that isn't a square?

revise.summary: Corresponding angles equal ⇔ lines parallel: both directions are true. Other converses fail: equal angles don't make a square, equal diagonals don't make a rectangle, and IE = IF doesn't force AB = AC.
focus: Test converses about lines and quadrilaterals.
remember: Rectangle: all angles equal but not a square.
Equal diagonals bisecting each other → rectangle; plus perpendicular → square.
Isosceles trapezium: equal diagonals, not a rectangle.
∠A = 60°, ∠B = 90°, ∠C = 30°: IE = IF but AB ≠ AC.
traps: Writing the inverse is not writing the converse.
Equal diagonals that bisect each other give a rectangle, not a rhombus.
Nearly equal angles do not make lines parallel.

topics.title: Equations, squares and products: which way works?

learn.hook: If x = y, then x² = y². But if x² = y², is x = y? Try x = −4 and y = 4!
points: If a = b, then a + c = b + c (adding the same number keeps equality). The converse, cancellation, is also true: if a + c = b + c, then a = b.
If x = y, then x² = y² is true, but the converse is false: (−3)² = 3² while −3 ≠ 3.
If x = y, then x³ = y³, and the converse is also true for real numbers: cubes keep the sign, so equal cubes mean equal numbers.
The product of two perfect squares is a perfect square: a² × b² = (ab)². The converse fails: 2 × 8 = 16 is a perfect square, but 2 and 8 are not.

example.q: Is the converse of 'If x = y then x³ = y³' true? Check with x³ = −27.
steps: x³ = −27 only for x = −3 (real numbers)
No other real number cubes to −27
So x³ = y³ gives x = y: converse true

learn.reallife: Balancing scales: add the same weight to both pans and they stay balanced; that is equality preserved by addition.

games.title: Which way works?
items: If a + 5 = b + 5, then a = b.
Subtract 5 from both sides (cancellation).
If x² = y², then x = y.
If x³ = y³, then x = y (real numbers).
Cubes keep the sign, so they are one-to-one.
If a × b is a perfect square, then a and b are perfect squares.
If a and b are perfect squares, then ab is a perfect square.
a = m², b = n² gives ab = (mn)².

items.text: x² = y² but x ≠ y: x = 5, y = ___
ab square, a and b not: a = 3, b = ___

quiz.q: 'If a = b, then a + 7 = b + 7.' What is its converse, and is it true?
options: If a + 7 = b + 7 then a = b; true
If a ≠ b then a + 7 ≠ b + 7; false
If a + 7 = b, then a = b + 7; true
quiz.explain: Subtracting 7 from both sides gives the converse: cancellation.
steps: Converse: 'If a + 7 = b + 7, then a = b.'
Subtract 7 from both sides: a = b. True (cancellation).
Answer: If a + 7 = b + 7 then a = b; true
quiz.mistake: Writes a different statement instead of swapping hypothesis and conclusion

quiz.q: Which pair shows that 'If x² = y², then x = y' is false?
quiz.explain: Both squares are 36 but the numbers differ.
steps: We need x² = y² but x ≠ y.
Answer: x = −6, y = 6
quiz.mistake: Picks a pair where x = y

quiz.q: Is 'If x³ = y³, then x = y' true for real numbers?
options: No, x = −2, y = 2 is a counterexample
No, cubes can be equal for different numbers
quiz.explain: (−2)³ = −8 and 2³ = 8 differ; cubes keep the sign, so equal cubes force equal numbers.
steps: Cubes keep the sign: (−2)³ = −8, 2³ = 8.
So different real numbers have different cubes.
Equal cubes force equal numbers.
Answer: Yes
quiz.mistake: Wrongly copies the counterexample from squares

quiz.q: Which statement and converse are BOTH true?
options: ab square and a, b squares
quiz.explain: Only the cube statement works both ways.
steps: x² = y² ⇏ x = y (−3, 3); 2 × 8 = 16 but 2, 8 not squares; a > b ⇏ a² > b² for negatives.
x = y ⇔ x³ = y³ works both ways.
Answer: x = y and x³ = y³
quiz.mistake: Thinks squaring works both ways

quiz.q: Which pair is a counterexample to 'If ab is a perfect square, then a and b are perfect squares'?
quiz.explain: 3 × 27 = 81 = 9², but neither 3 nor 27 is a perfect square.
steps: We need ab a perfect square but a, b not both squares.
3 × 27 = 81 = 9², and neither 3 nor 27 is a square.
4, 9, 1, 16, 25 are all squares.
Answer: 3 and 27
quiz.mistake: Picks two perfect squares

quiz.q: Why is the product of two perfect squares always a perfect square?
options: Because m² + n² is a square
quiz.explain: Rearranging the factors gives a square of mn.
steps: m² × n² = m × m × n × n.
Rearrange: (m × n) × (m × n) = (mn)².
Answer: m² × n² = (mn)²
quiz.mistake: Confuses product with sum

quiz.q: If x² = 49, what are the possible values of x?
quiz.explain: Both 7² and (−7)² equal 49.
steps: So x = 7 or x = −7.
Answer: 7 or −7
quiz.mistake: Forgets the negative root

quiz.q: Kiran writes: 'a + 3 = b + 3, so a = b.' Which property is he using?
options: Cancellation (the converse of adding the same number)
quiz.explain: Subtracting 3 from both sides undoes adding 3.
steps: From a + 3 = b + 3, subtract 3 from both sides.
This undoes adding 3: cancellation.
Answer: Cancellation (the converse of adding the same number)
quiz.mistake: Names an unrelated property

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If x² = y², does that mean x = y?"
teach.praise: Correct! x = −3 and y = 3 have equal squares but are different numbers!
teach.nudge: Can you think of two different numbers with the same square?

revise.summary: Adding the same number keeps equality and cancellation reverses it. x = y ⇒ x² = y² has a false converse, but x = y ⇔ x³ = y³. A product of squares is a square, but not conversely.
focus: Decide which operations work in both directions.
Find counterexamples for squares and products.
Solve x² = k with both roots.
remember: (−3)² = 3², so squares can hide signs.
Cubes keep the sign: equal cubes mean equal numbers.
a² × b² = (ab)²; 2 × 8 = 16 shows the converse fails.
traps: Don't forget the negative root.
Squaring does not work both ways.
Product of squares is not about sums.

learn.hook: Every number divisible by 24 is divisible by 6. Is every number divisible by 6 divisible by 24? Try 12!
points: 'If n is divisible by 24, then n is divisible by 4 and by 6' is true. Its converse is false: 12 is divisible by 4 and 6 but not by 24 (because LCM(4, 6) = 12, not 24).
'n is divisible by 60 if and only if it is divisible by 5 and by 12' is true both ways, because 5 and 12 share no factor and LCM(5, 12) = 60.
'Divisible by 8 ⇒ divisible by 2 and 4' is true; the converse fails: 4 and 12 are divisible by 2 and 4 but not by 8.
Test for 8: a number is divisible by 8 if and only if the number formed by its last three digits is, because 1000 = 8 × 125.
Test for 3: if the digit sum is divisible by 3 the number is, and conversely; both directions are true.

example.q: Is 7,35,136 divisible by 8? Use the last three digits.
steps: Last three digits: 136
So 735136 is divisible by 8

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers packing items in boxes of 8 can check if a big order fits exactly using the last-three-digits test.

games.title: Divisibility logic
items: If n is divisible by 24, it is divisible by 6.
If n is divisible by 4 and 6, it is divisible by 24.
12 is a counterexample.
If n is divisible by 5 and 12, it is divisible by 60.
If the digit sum of n is divisible by 3, then n is divisible by 3.
This is the test for 3.
If n is divisible by 2 and 4, it is divisible by 8.
4 itself is a counterexample.

quiz.q: Which number is a counterexample to 'If n is divisible by 4 and 6, then n is divisible by 24'?
quiz.explain: 36 is divisible by 4 and 6 but 36 ÷ 24 = 1.5.
steps: We need divisible by 4 and 6 but not by 24.
48, 24 and 72 are multiples of 24.
Answer: 36
quiz.mistake: Picks a multiple of 24

quiz.q: Why is 'divisible by 5 and 12 ⇒ divisible by 60' true?
options: 5 and 12 have no common factor, so LCM(5, 12) = 60
quiz.explain: A number divisible by both is divisible by their LCM, which here is the product.
steps: Divisible by 5 and 12 means divisible by LCM(5, 12).
5 and 12 share no factor, so LCM = 5 × 12 = 60.
Answer: 5 and 12 have no common factor, so LCM(5, 12) = 60
quiz.mistake: Thinks it holds for any two divisors

quiz.q: What is LCM(4, 6)?
quiz.explain: Multiples of 6: 6, 12; 12 is also a multiple of 4.
steps: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, ...
12 is the first that is also a multiple of 4.
Answer: 12
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the numbers instead

quiz.q: Is 4,61,720 divisible by 8?
quiz.explain: Only the last three digits matter: 720.
steps: Test for 8: look at the last three digits.
720 = 8 × 90, so it is divisible by 8.
Answer: Yes, 720 = 8 × 90
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong digits for the test

quiz.q: Why does the last-three-digits test for 8 work?
options: 1000 is divisible by 8, so only the last three digits affect the remainder
Every number ends in three digits
It works only for even numbers
quiz.explain: Any number = 1000 × (something) + last three digits.
steps: Any number = 1000 × (front part) + last three digits.
1000 = 8 × 125, so the front part adds nothing to the remainder.
Answer: 1000 is divisible by 8, so only the last three digits affect the remainder
quiz.mistake: Cannot explain why the test works

quiz.q: Which number shows 'divisible by 2 and 4 ⇒ divisible by 8' is false?
quiz.explain: 20 is divisible by 2 and 4 but not by 8.
steps: We need divisible by 2 and 4 but not by 8.
16, 40, 24 are multiples of 8.
Answer: 20
quiz.mistake: Picks a multiple of 8

quiz.q: The four-digit number 47d2 (d is a single digit) is divisible by 3. Which value of d works?
quiz.explain: Digit sum = 4 + 7 + d + 2 = 13 + d. With d = 2 it is 15, a multiple of 3; with 3, 4 or 6 it is 16, 17 or 19.
steps: Answer: 2
quiz.mistake: Adds the digits wrongly

quiz.q: 'If a number is divisible by 3, then its digit sum is divisible by 3.' Is this converse of the digit-sum test true?
options: No, it works only for even numbers
Yes, both directions of the test for 3 are true
quiz.explain: A number and its digit sum leave the same remainder when divided by 3, so both directions hold.
steps: A number and its digit sum leave the same remainder on division by 3.
So divisible by 3 ⇔ digit sum divisible by 3.
Both directions hold (12: digit sum 3 ✓).
Answer: Yes, both directions of the test for 3 are true
quiz.mistake: Assumes every converse fails

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If a number is divisible by 4 and by 6, must it be divisible by 24?"
teach.praise: Brilliant! 12 is divisible by 4 and 6 but not 24, because LCM(4, 6) = 12!
teach.nudge: Can you find a small number divisible by both 4 and 6 but not by 24?

revise.summary: Divisible by 24 ⇒ divisible by 4 and 6, but not conversely, since LCM(4, 6) = 12. Divisible by 5 and 12 ⇔ divisible by 60. The tests for 8 (last three digits) and 3 (digit sum) work both ways.
focus: Use LCMs to decide divisibility converses.
remember: LCM(4, 6) = 12, so 12 or 36 break the converse.
1000 = 8 × 125, so check the last three digits: 7,35,136 → 136 = 8 × 17.
traps: Being divisible by two numbers means divisible by their LCM, not their product.
Use the last three digits for 8, not the last digit.
Not every converse fails.

learn.hook: n² + n + 11 gives 13, 17, 23, 31, 41, ... all primes! Keep going and it breaks at n = 10.
points: Any common factor of n and n + 3 must divide their difference 3, so it is 1 or 3.
So: if n and n + 3 have no common factor (other than 1), then n is not a multiple of 3. Conversely, if n is not a multiple of 3, then n and n + 3 share no factor. Both directions are true.
Formulas that seem to give only primes can fail: 4n² + 1 gives 5, 17, 37, then 65 = 5 × 13 at n = 4.
n² + n + 11 fails at n = 10: 121 = 11². 2ⁿ − 1 with n prime fails at n = 11: 2047 = 23 × 89. 2ⁿ + 1 fails at n = 3: 9.
Many examples never prove a statement, but one counterexample disproves it.

example.q: Does n² + n + 11 always give a prime? Test n = 10.
steps: Not prime, so the claim is false

learn.reallife: Computer security uses huge primes, so mathematicians must be careful: a formula that 'usually' gives primes is not good enough.

games.title: Do n and n + 3 share a factor > 1?

quiz.q: What is the smallest n ≥ 1 for which 4n² + 1 is not prime?
steps: Answer: 4
quiz.mistake: Stops checking too early

quiz.q: For n = 10, what is n² + n + 11?
steps: n² + n + 11 with n = 10.
Answer: 121
quiz.mistake: Forgets one of the terms

quiz.q: 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047. Which shows it is not prime?
steps: So 2047 is not prime.
quiz.mistake: Assumes 2ᵖ − 1 is always prime for prime p

quiz.q: Which value of n is a counterexample to '2ⁿ + 1 is always prime'?
steps: 2³ + 1 = 9 = 3 × 3: not prime.
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Picks a value that gives a prime

quiz.q: Any common factor of n and n + 3 must divide:
quiz.explain: If d divides both, it divides (n + 3) − n = 3.
steps: If d divides n and n + 3, it divides their difference.
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Does not use the difference

quiz.q: Do 21 and 24 have a common factor greater than 1?
options: Yes, 3, because 21 is a multiple of 3
steps: Both are multiples of 3 (here n = 21 is a multiple of 3).
Answer: Yes, 3, because 21 is a multiple of 3
quiz.mistake: Forgets that n = 21 is a multiple of 3

quiz.q: n = 20 is not a multiple of 3. What can you say about 20 and 23?
options: They have no common factor except 1
quiz.explain: The only possible common factor is 3, and 3 does not divide 20.
steps: The only possible common factor of n and n + 3 is 1 or 3.
3 does not divide 20.
So 20 and 23 share only 1.
Answer: They have no common factor except 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks even numbers always share factors

quiz.q: Ravi checks n² + n + 11 for n = 1 to 9 and gets primes every time. What can he conclude?
options: It gives primes for all odd n
It is proved for n up to 100
Nothing for all n; checking examples does not prove it, and n = 10 fails
quiz.explain: Examples can suggest a pattern but cannot prove it.
steps: Examples can suggest a pattern but cannot prove it for all n.
n = 10 gives 121 = 11², not prime.
Answer: Nothing for all n; checking examples does not prove it, and n = 10 fails
quiz.mistake: Treats many examples as a proof

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "A formula gave primes 9 times in a row. Does it always give primes?"
teach.praise: Exactly! Examples never prove it, and one counterexample breaks it!
teach.nudge: Is checking a few cases enough? What would show the formula is wrong?

revise.summary: Common factors of n and n + 3 must divide 3. Formulas that seem to give only primes can fail, so examples never prove a pattern but one counterexample disproves it.
focus: Use differences to find common factors.
Explain why examples are not proof.
remember: n and n + 3 share no factor ⇔ n not a multiple of 3.
4n² + 1 fails at n = 4 (65); n² + n + 11 fails at n = 10 (121).
traps: Don't stop checking too early.
2ᵖ − 1 is not always prime for prime p.
Many examples are not a proof.

learn.hook: Kabir checked 100 examples and says his rule always works. A mathematician smiles: 'Show me a proof that covers ALL numbers, even the ones you didn't try!'
points: A proof is a chain of logical steps that shows a statement is true in every case, starting from facts already accepted.
Axioms are basic facts accepted without proof. Theorems are statements that have been proved. A conjecture is believed true but not yet proved.
Checking examples can suggest a pattern, but it can never prove a statement about all numbers.
Use algebra to cover all cases: an even number is 2m and an odd number is 2m + 1, for some integer m.
To disprove a statement about all cases, one counterexample is enough.

example.q: Prove that the sum of two odd numbers is always even.
steps: Let the odd numbers be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1, where m and n are integers
This is 2 times an integer, so it is even, whatever m and n are
example.answer: The sum is 2(m + n + 1), which is always even.

learn.reallife: Online banking is safe because of number facts that mathematicians have proved. Engineers rely on proved results, not lucky guesses, to make bridges stand.

games.title: Prove: odd + odd = even
items: Let the numbers be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1
Add them: 2m + 2n + 2
Take out 2: 2(m + n + 1)
2 times an integer is even, so the sum is even

games.title: Words of proof
pairs: Axiom
A basic fact accepted without proof
Theorem
A statement that has been proved
Conjecture
Believed to be true but not yet proved
Counterexample
One case that shows a claim is false
Converse
Statement with hypothesis and conclusion swapped

quiz.q: Kabir checks 1 + 3 = 4, 3 + 5 = 8 and 5 + 7 = 12, and says: 'The sum of two odd numbers is always even. Proved!' What is wrong?
options: Nothing, three examples are a proof
Examples alone cannot prove a statement for all numbers
quiz.explain: The statement is true, but checking a few cases is not a proof. A proof must work for every pair of odd numbers, for example using 2m + 1 and 2n + 1.
steps: The statement is true, but three examples do not cover every case.
A proof must work for all odd numbers, e.g. using 2m + 1 and 2n + 1.
Answer: Examples alone cannot prove a statement for all numbers
quiz.mistake: Believes that enough examples make a proof

quiz.q: Which expression stands for any odd number, if m is an integer?
quiz.explain: 2m is always even, so one more than it, 2m + 1, is always odd.
steps: 2m is always even.
One more than an even number is odd: 2m + 1.
m + 1 is even when m is odd.
Answer: 2m + 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks m + 1 is always odd, but it is even when m is odd

quiz.q: The sum of three consecutive integers n, n + 1, n + 2 is 3n + 3. Which number always divides this sum?
quiz.explain: 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1), so the sum is always a multiple of 3. It is not always even: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.
steps: Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Generalises from 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 and says 6

quiz.q: What do we call a basic fact that is accepted without proof?
quiz.explain: Axioms are the starting points of reasoning; theorems are proved from them.
steps: Axioms are accepted without proof.
Theorems are proved; conjectures are unproved beliefs.
Answer: An axiom
quiz.mistake: Mixes up theorems (proved) with axioms (assumed)

quiz.q: (2m + 1)(2n + 1) = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1. What does this prove about the product of two odd numbers?
options: It is always a multiple of 4
quiz.explain: 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1, which is one more than an even number, so it is odd.
steps: That is an even number plus 1.
So the product of two odd numbers is always odd.
Answer: It is always odd
quiz.mistake: Sees the even terms 4mn, 2m and 2n and forgets the + 1

quiz.q: Goldbach's conjecture says every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. What is its status?
options: It has been checked for very many numbers but not yet proved
It has been shown false by a counterexample
quiz.explain: Computers have checked it for enormous numbers, but nobody has found a proof yet, so it is still a conjecture.
steps: Goldbach's conjecture has been checked for very many numbers.
Nobody has proved it, so it is still a conjecture.
Answer: It has been checked for very many numbers but not yet proved
quiz.mistake: Thinks checking very many cases turns a conjecture into a theorem

quiz.q: How many counterexamples are needed to show that a statement about all numbers is false?
quiz.explain: A claim about ALL cases fails as soon as one case breaks it.
steps: A claim about all cases fails if one case breaks it.
So one counterexample is enough.
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks you need many failures to disprove a general claim

quiz.q: In the usual proof that the angles of a triangle add up to 180°, a line is drawn through one vertex parallel to the opposite side. Which fact is used next?
options: Alternate angles made by a transversal with parallel lines are equal
The diagonals of a square are equal
quiz.explain: The two alternate angles equal two angles of the triangle, and together with the third angle they form a straight angle of 180°.
steps: Draw a line through a vertex parallel to the opposite side.
Alternate angles with the parallel lines equal two of the triangle's angles.
These with the third angle form a straight angle: 180°.
Answer: Alternate angles made by a transversal with parallel lines are equal
quiz.mistake: Tries to use a special triangle instead of facts that work for every triangle

teach.ask: Gappu tested 50 pairs of even numbers and their sum was always even: "Isn't that a proof?"
teach.praise: Examples are not enough: a proof must cover every case. Using 2m + 2n = 2(m + n) proves it for all even numbers at once!
teach.nudge: What about the numbers you didn't test? How can you show it works for every even number?

revise.summary: A proof is a chain of logical steps showing a statement is true in every case. Axioms are accepted, theorems are proved and conjectures are unproved. Algebra (2m, 2m + 1) covers all cases.
focus: Prove simple number facts with algebra.
Tell axioms, theorems and conjectures apart.
remember: Even = 2m, odd = 2m + 1.
Odd + odd = 2(m + n + 1), even.
Odd × odd = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1, odd.
Goldbach's conjecture is checked but not proved.
traps: Checking examples is not a proof.
m + 1 is not always odd.
Checking many cases does not make a conjecture a theorem.
